item.title: China expresses 'serious concern' over UK's unfounded 'cyber challenge' claims regarding Chinese AI
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 16:28:00
Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning China expresses serious concern over the UK's use of speculative language to smear China without evidence, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday, calling the relevant UK authorities' claims of a cyber threat posed by China's artificial intelligence (AI) counterproductive to China-UK mutual trust and harmful to the UK's credibility in global AI cooperation. At a regular press briefing in Beijing, Mao Ning, the spokesperson, was asked to comment on reports that the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, part of the Government Communications Headquarters, had claimed that China, as a major power in AI, is "highly likely" to frequently use AI to carry out hacking operations by 2028 and poses the "most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the UK." Noting that the Chinese side has noticed relevant reports, Mao said that regrettably, the UK has long politicized cybersecurity issues and is now pouring the "new wine" of suppressing China's AI development into the "old bottle" of "cyberattacks." "Such erroneous practice will not help enhance mutual trust between China and the UK, and will also damage the UK's credibility in global cooperation on AI safety governance," Mao said. Cybersecurity risks arising from AI are a common challenge facing all countries, and new international rules should be formulated under the framework of the United Nations to address these challenges collectively, Mao said. China has consistently maintained that AI development should be guided by the principles of pursuing progress, promoting good, openness and inclusiveness, while balancing security and development to ensure that AI remains safe, reliable and controllable, Mao said. Global Times

item.title: Taiwan region can attend APEC meeting by following one-China principle, relevant MoU and practices: mainland spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 14:44:00
Zhu Fenglian Photo: Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council Taiwan region can participate in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting as long as it follows the one-China principle, relevant provisions of APEC memorandum of understanding (MoU), and established practices, a Chinese mainland spokesperson said on Wednesday, in response to claims made by the Taiwan regional authorities. At a press conference, Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, was asked to comment on claims made by Taiwan regional authorities that an invitation to this year's APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting was sent to Taiwan region via email instead of a letter, and the mainland has given Taiwan region "differential treatment." In response, Zhu said that the Chinese mainland has consistently handled matters concerning the Taiwan region's participation in APEC meetings in accordance with the one-China principle, relevant provisions of APEC MoU and established practices. "As long as the abovementioned practices are followed, the Taiwan region can participate in the meeting," Zhu stated. Global Times

item.title: Chinese business group welcomes EU approval of Germany's Ceconomy acquisition, saying it underscores value of dialogue
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 13:14:00
The European Union flags in front of EU headquarters in Brussels, Belgium. Photo: Xinhua The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU (CCCEU) said on Wednesday that it welcomes European Commission's approval of Chinese e-commerce giant JD.com's acquisition of Germany's Ceconomy Group under the bloc's Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR). A Chinese analyst said the move is conducive to fostering commercial interests among Chinese and EU companies, and urged the bloc to foster a fair, transparent, and non-discriminatory market environment so that Chinese companies' interest in the bloc is not undermined. The decision, reached after extensive engagement with both parties and a comprehensive assessment of the proposed commitments, underscores the importance of constructive dialogue between regulators and businesses in addressing regulatory concerns, the CCCEU said in a statement. EC's approval was made on Tuesday. According to Reuters, the acquisition will help one of China's largest retailers to expand outside its home market via Ceconomy-owned electronic products retailers MediaMarkt and Saturn. This marks the first case in which an acquisition by a Chinese company has been approved by the EC following an in-depth investigation under the FSR. The EC decision came amid frequent and ongoing bilateral communications and talks over economic and trade issues, with the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism recently yielding positive progress and a number of consensuses. However, the CCCEU pointed out that the FSR and its implementation remain a key concern for Chinese companies investing in Europe and it expects the EU to uphold the principles of objectivity, fairness, transparency and proportionality in enforcing and implementing the FSR. "Regulatory measures should be tailored to the circumstances of each case, with due regard for businesses' legitimate rights and interests, and should not create unnecessary barriers to legitimate commercial investment or market cooperation," it said. Zhang Jian, a vice president of the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, told the Global Times on Wednesday that the EC's latest has a positive significance, demonstrating that the importance of constructive dialogue between regulators and businesses in addressing regulatory concerns and the proper handling of the case is conducive to the win-win commercial cooperation between companies from both sides. However, whether this will set a template for future FSR cases involving Chinese companies remains to be seen, since the underlying logic of the EU's trade and economic policy toward China has not changed, Zhang said. He noted that the bloc should keep its market fair and objective and avoid discriminating against Chinese companies operating in the EU given their contribution to the EU's growth and job creation. The transaction is expected to bring fresh investment, digital expertise, logistics capabilities and supply chain resources to Europe's retail sector, supporting local business development and innovation while creating new opportunities for commercial cooperation between Chinese and European companies, said the CCCEU. The chamber said it also encourages the EU to improve regulatory transparency and policy predictability, helping to ensure a fair, non-discriminatory, stable and predictable business environment for investors from all countries, including China. This would help boost Chinese companies' confidence in investing and growing their businesses in Europe, while supporting the healthy, stable and sustainable development of bilateral economic and trade relations, it said. Despite a series of economic and trade consultations, the EU is reportedly considering expanding trade restrictions to additional sectors including chemicals and machinery amid concerns over competition from Chinese imports. China will take all necessary measures to defend its legitimate rights and interests, if the EU persists in imposing discriminatory restrictions against Chinese products, a spokesperson of the Chinese Ministry of Commerce said on October 29. In May 2026, China's Ministry of Justice determined that the EU's cross-border investigative measures targeting Chinese security firm Nuctech under the FSR constitute improper extraterritorial jurisdiction.

item.title: Scholars from around the world trace Silk Road history in Xinjiang
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 12:43:00
A scholar from Pakistan shares research findings at the symposium titled Towards Anxi from Afar: Academic Symposium on Qiuci Studies, in Urumqi, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Oct. 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Yuanhao) Once a thriving crossroads on the Silk Road in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, the ancient kingdom of Kucha has left traces of its rich history in museums and collections around the world. Buddhist murals, sculptures and manuscripts from the Kucha kingdom, also known as the ancient Qiuci State ("Qiuci" being its Chinese pinyin form), are now held in Berlin, St. Petersburg, Tokyo and elsewhere. Reconstructing its past is therefore requiring researchers to work across borders and pool their expertise. Understanding Kucha's past has become an international scholarly effort. The shared pursuit brought more than 180 scholars from 15 countries and regions to Urumqi, capital of Xinjiang, for a two-day symposium, titled Towards Anxi from Afar: Academic Symposium on Qiuci Studies, which concluded on Sunday. Scholars from China, Britain, Germany, Italy, Japan, Pakistan and elsewhere exchanged research findings on ancient texts, religion, archaeology and cultural heritage conservation. Located between the Tianshan Mountains and the Taklimakan Desert, the ancient Kucha region encompassed parts of today's Kuqa, Baicheng, Xayar and Xinhe in Xinjiang. For centuries, it was a meeting point of civilizations. Chinese silk and paper traveled westward along trade routes, while Buddhism from India, Persian artistic influences and Sogdian merchants made their way east. At the symposium, Rong Xinjiang, a professor at Peking University and president of the Chinese Dunhuang-Turpan Society, presented new research on a tomb epitaph unearthed in Kuqa in 2025. For overseas researchers, keeping up with archaeological discoveries in Xinjiang is an important reason to maintain close ties with Chinese scholars. "Continued contact with colleagues around the world, especially in China, is essential," said Caren Dreyer, a researcher at the Museum of Asian Art in Berlin. "It enables us to keep abreast of new findings and to participate actively in the international scholarly community." For Erica Hunter, a scholar from the University of Cambridge who specializes in relics and Syriac manuscripts excavated from Turpan, the value of such gatherings lies in bringing together evidence that would otherwise remain separated by geography. Russian scholars can share materials from St. Petersburg, while German researchers can discuss those in Berlin, Hunter said. Equally important are the different interpretations scholars bring to their research. Hunter has visited Xinjiang several times over the past four years to share her research on Syriac manuscripts discovered in the region. She said such exchanges help scholars overcome barriers and learn from one another. "It's a two-way process, and that's very important." On his first visit to Xinjiang, Pakistani scholar Fawad Khan followed the presentations with keen interest. He said the symposium offered a valuable learning opportunity for scholars. The exchanges also reflected a growing emphasis on international collaboration in Silk Road studies, as Chinese institutions expand academic cooperation in fields ranging from Turpan and Qiuci studies, to research on the ancient city of Beiting. For Italian scholar Erica Forte, the symposium was also a reunion. Speaking Chinese with colleagues, she caught up with old friends and professors who had supported her during her studies. For her, the conversations reflected what had long given the Silk Road its significance, namely connections between people and cultures, as scholars came together to exchange findings, compare perspectives and deepen their understanding of a kingdom that once stood at the crossroads of civilizations. Erica Hunter, a scholar from the University of Cambridge, attends the symposium titled Towards Anxi from Afar: Academic Symposium on Qiuci Studies, in Urumqi, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Oct. 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Yuanhao)

item.title: Silver-haired Chinese take up AI, video editing and drones
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 11:37:00
This undated photo shows the elderly taking a short video production class at Ningxia University for the Elderly in Yinchuan, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. (Xinhua) Zhao Minghui, 71, took notes of the tutor's guidance with a pen, listing how to use artificial intelligence (AI) applications on her smartphone. "We may be getting older, but we still want to keep up with the times," said Zhao after the class at Ningxia University for the Elderly in northwest China. Zhao used to ask her children for help with her smartphone. After enrolling in the university's classes, she learned to send WeChat messages, make mobile payments, book tickets and medical appointments, and edit short videos, all on her smartphone. This year, she registered for the AI course. Instructor Yu Cheng recalled that roughly 60 to 70 percent of his students could not use smartphones back in 2019 when he started teaching there. Today, he rarely encounters such students. "Type in a sentence, and it can generate text or pictures," said the amazed Zhao, who now uses AI for answering questions and even chatting when she feels bored. Across China, universities for the elderly are offering AI, video production and drone photography courses, helping retirees handle everyday tasks more easily, keep in touch with family or simply try something new. China had more than 323 million people aged 60 and above by 2025, accounting for 23 percent of its population. However, only 53.7 percent of that age group were internet users, compared with a national internet penetration rate of 80.1 percent, official figures showed. Wang Weiyu, 69, is among those applying new skills for creation in eastern China's Shandong Province. At Qingdao University for the Elderly, instructor Ji Pengcheng mirrored his smartphone screen onto a large display, showing about a dozen students how to edit videos. When someone struggled with an operation, he walked over to help. Wang enrolled in the class earlier this year. In six months, she has learned to use editing software, camera techniques and video templates. "Whenever I share a self-made video clip in my family WeChat group, the children always give me a thumbs-up," she said, smiling. Such enthusiasm among learners has fueled surging demand for tech courses at universities for the elderly nationwide. In 2025, all 60 places in a DeepSeek AI course at a university for the elderly in Guangzhou were snapped up within tens of seconds upon registration. In Shanghai, the university for the elderly has enrolled students even in their 80s on drone photography courses, which were launched in 2022. At Ningxia University for the Elderly, more than 3,600 people have registered for technology courses, covering AI applications, video production, smart home technology and e-commerce. "Many courses fill up within minutes of registration opening," said Liu Rui, deputy director of the university's service center. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for expanding educational opportunities for older people and developing more universities for the elderly to meet their cultural and intellectual needs. For many participants, the appeal goes beyond learning new practical skills, with classes also providing opportunities for personal growth and social interaction. "Learning these new skills has made my retirement more fulfilling," said Xu Zonggang, a 70-year-old in Qingdao, who is planning his next trip with classmates. The elderly learn the use of drones at a university for the elderly in Qingdao, east China's Shandong Province, Sept. 23, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Aoqiu)

item.title: Uzbek president's new book highlights shared development vision with China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 00:20:00
The Chinese version of a new book by Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev titled "Uzbekistan on the Path to Sustainable Development and Prosperity" A new book by Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, presented in its Chinese-language edition in Beijing on October 30, highlights the shared development vision and growing cooperation between China and Uzbekistan, offering Chinese readers insights into Uzbekistan's domestic reforms, foreign policy and development priorities. The Embassy of the Republic of Uzbekistan in China presented the Chinese version of a new book by Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev on October 30 in Beijing. Titled "Uzbekistan on the Path to Sustainable Development and Prosperity," the book highlights the shared governance philosophy and aligned development strategy in both Uzbekistan and China. In his address, Uzbek Ambassador to China Farhod Arziev said that the book brings together speeches by the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan on domestic and foreign policy, as well as interviews and articles published in foreign media during the period from 2021 to 2025. These materials reflect the comprehensive reforms being implemented to build a New Uzbekistan. This book will undoubtedly serve as an important source of information for Chinese and international audiences about the far-reaching reforms being implemented in Uzbekistan under the leadership of the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan, the development of New Uzbekistan, and the key priorities of the country's domestic and foreign policy, said Arziev. Published by China's prestigious People's Publishing House, the book will be distributed to China's central government institutions, higher education institutions, national and regional libraries, research and analytical institutions, cultural and humanitarian centers, and media organizations, Ambassador Arziev said. Olim Davlatov, advisor to the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan, gives a speech at the launch ceremony in Beijing on October 30, 2026. Photos: Courtesy of the Embassy of the Republic of Uzbekistan in China During his speech, Olim Davlatov, advisor to the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan, said that the book covers the issues of the president of the Republic of Uzbekistan Shavkat Miromonovich Mirziyoev in 2021-25, large-scale reforms in Uzbekistan, the activities of Uzbekistan within the United Nations and Shanghai Cooperation Organization, regional cooperation, sustainable development and economic diplomacy. The book's coverage of relations with China is of particular importance for understating the substance and development of the cooperation of China and Uzbekistan, said Davlatov. The political will, mutual trust and regular dialogue of the leaders of Uzbekistan and China have elevated bilateral relations to a high level, Davlatov noted. Odiljon Tojiev, chairman of the Board of the National Media Association of Uzbekistan and member of the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis, said that in recent years, relations between Uzbekistan and China have reached a new stage. "Today, our bilateral ties continue to develop steadily on the basis of mutual respect, trust and shared development goals," said Tojiev. The transformation being carried out under the leadership of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev is focused on human dignity, the well-being of the people and the building of a just society, Tojiev said. Talking about the alignment in development strategy between China and Uzbekistan, Tojiev said that both countries are steadily implementing strategies aimed at advancing digitalization, promoting environmental sustainability and improving quality of life. These include China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for national economic and social development and Uzbekistan's "Uzbekistan-2030" Strategy.

item.title: The 'myth' of Western-style democracy is losing its appeal even in the West: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 00:09:00
Demonstrators face off with law enforcement officers during a protest in Paris, France, on October 17, 2026. Photo: Xinhua The most fundamental and significant standard for evaluating whether a democracy is good is whether it can consistently provide the populace with stable livelihoods, clear expectations, and hopeful prospects. A poll released by the Pew Research Center this year shows that public satisfaction with how democracy works in their own countries is declining dramatically. Dissatisfaction rate stands at 69 percent in France, 68 percent in Spain, 62 percent in Italy, 47 percent in Poland and 69 percent in the US. In fact, sustained tracking by several other prominent Western polling organizations, including Ipsos and Gallup, points to the same trend: Dissatisfaction with the functioning of democracy in Western countries is evolving from isolated discontent into a widespread public sentiment. This dissatisfaction is not merely reflected in polling figures; it is also visible on the streets across the Western world. Each Western country has its own set of problems. Some are plagued by frequent changes in political leadership, while others remain mired in the challenges of immigrant integration. Some are grappling with the painful effects of the energy transition and the steady decline of traditional industries, while others are struggling to contain increasingly intense social divisions. Yet polling data reveal a common thread running through public sentiment: More and more people no longer believe their governments genuinely represent the interests of ordinary citizens, or that existing political systems are capable of delivering meaningful change. Calls for fighting corruption, strengthening accountability, making public policies more responsive and ensuring that ordinary people's voices are genuinely heard have become shared demands across party lines and social classes in Western societies. Many once believed that voting was the entirety of democracy: As long as electoral procedures were followed, the outcome was legitimate and the popular will would naturally find its way into policymaking. But a growing number of people in Western countries are now realizing that voting is more like a periodic ritual. Making a choice once every few years does not guarantee that people will continue to have a say in public affairs in their daily lives between elections. According to a relevant OECD survey released this year, 68 percent of respondents believe that voting in an election has a significant or moderate influence on what government does, but only 31 percent are confident that people like them have a say in what government does. When people seeking to have their concerns addressed find that their votes often fail to translate into policy responses, their confidence in democracy naturally erodes in the face of reality. Current discussions among some Western elites about "what has gone wrong with democracy" often veer toward two one-sided explanations: either blaming all the problems on agitation by populists or attributing public dissatisfaction to a "loss of patience" with democracy. Both explanations evade a basic fact: The dissatisfaction with democracy in Western countries does not stem from misunderstanding, but from the failure of existing democratic institutions to respond effectively to public demands and meet societal needs. Following the end of the Cold War, Western countries experienced a period of relative social stability. At that time, the legitimacy of Western democracy did not derive from the so-called "end of history," but rested on the West's dominant advantages across multiple fields. As globalization accelerated, capital mobility increased, and industrial production was restructured, Western governments found their ability to redistribute wealth increasingly constrained by systemic pressures. Meanwhile, institutional corruption has increasingly permeated political processes, further exposing the inherent flaws of Western democratic systems. At its core, the dissatisfaction among Western populations is not a denial of democratic values, but rather a profound disappointment with the practice of democracy in the West. Some political parties in the West are increasingly leaning their policymaking toward capital interests, while the livelihood issues of ordinary people are being set aside. Electoral politics is gradually deteriorating into a power struggle between different elite factions, with partisan conflicts, veto politics, and policy flip-flops becoming the norm. The gap between political promises and reality continues to widen. The discontent from the grassroots is continuously questioning the practical adaptability of Western democratic systems, sowing further uncertainty for the future trajectory of Western politics. For most countries, the truly beneficial insight from the Western reflection on "what has gone wrong with democracy" is that there has never been a one-size-fits-all institutional form, nor is there a democratic model that can operate independently from its local soil and the genuine needs of its people. If votes are long treated as the entirety of democracy, if party interests are placed above the public good, and if slogans replace actual governance, then no matter how glossy the institutional facade, it will ultimately be discarded amid the repeated disappointments of the populace. The most fundamental and significant standard for evaluating whether a democracy is good is whether it can consistently provide the populace with stable livelihoods, clear expectations, and hopeful prospects. Unfortunately, some Western politicians and media continue to use democracy as a political instrument for export, seeking to arbitrarily draw ideological dividing lines, form blocs and provoke ideological confrontation on the international stage. This approach not only fails to truly respond to the demands of their own citizens but also exacerbates the disconnection between democracy and reality. As a result, the credibility of Western democracy continues to erode under the dual pressures of domestic livelihood crises and external hegemonic actions, ultimately leading to a trust crisis both at home and abroad.

item.title: Once Japan acquires nuclear weapons, it will surely bite the hand that feeds it
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 23:36:00
Protesters hold a banner during a rally in Tokyo, Japan, on November 21, 2025, after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi criticized the country's traditional policy against nuclear weapons. Photo: VCG Just as Tokyo shows signs of breaking through its "Three Non-Nuclear Principles," some individuals have "conveniently" offered up a bad idea. According to Japanese media reports on Tuesday, some experts in Washington, including a US Navy official, have suggested that Tokyo "should consider acquiring nuclear submarines," with the aim of "enabling the Japan Self-Defense Forces to deter China more effectively." However, these American "experts" are nothing but Washington's "liability." Since the Sanae Takaichi administration took office, certain Japanese politicians have become obsessed with "acquiring nuclear‑powered submarines." Japan's Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has repeatedly and publicly advocated for the introduction of nuclear-powered submarines. In their narrative, nuclear‑powered submarines represent nothing more than an upgrade in propulsion and do not equate to carrying nuclear weapons - a word game they hope will allow them to pursue their agenda. However, the fuel cycle, spent fuel reprocessing, and nuclear material controls for nuclear-powered submarines substantially overlap with pathways for developing nuclear weapons. Japan already stockpiles large quantities of separated plutonium and has well-established reserves of nuclear material, reactor-technology expertise and delivery-platform foundations. Should Tokyo achieve the technical and political breakthrough of "introducing nuclear-powered submarines," no insurmountable technical gap would stand in the way of it later developing its own nuclear warheads. "Buy the submarines first, then acquire nuclear-weapon capability" is the roadmap quietly plotted by Japan's right-wing forces. The US is aware of these risks, yet it has long turned a blind eye. Some US politicians harbor opportunistic calculations regarding Tokyo: They want to arm Japan as their forward‑edge spearhead in East Asia and make Japan bear more of the costs of confrontation. They imagine they hold the reins and can keep this "proxy tool" firmly in check to prevent it from turning on its master. This mind-set is steeped in short‑sighted arrogance. In essence, it gambles with the postwar international order and the non‑proliferation regime, allowing the dangerous "Pandora's box" to be slowly opened for the sake of short-term geopolitical gains. Washington fantasizes that "limited rearmament of Japan" will serve its own strategy, but it underestimates the tenacity of Japan's right‑wing forces to shake off constraints. After Japan's defeat in World War II, segments of its right‑wing have relied on the US security umbrella while harboring deep‑seated resentment and frustration over the "humiliation of being bombed." Meanwhile, tens of thousands of US troops stationed in Japan serve both as a platform for US power projection and as shackles on Japan. Japan's current willingness to dance to Washington's tune stems from its insufficient strength for full independence; it needs US acquiescence to loosen restrictions. Such compliance is tactical pretense for the time being, not permanent submission. It's obvious that if Japan crosses the bottom line and truly acquires nuclear‑deterrence capacity, it will never resign itself to being a US "outpost" forever. Should the US continue to indulge Japan in challenging the "Three Non-Nuclear Principles" and allow nuclear‑related capabilities to take root on Japanese soil, it will eventually reap what it sows. If Japan possesses nuclear weapons, it will surely bite the hand that feeds it.

item.title: GT Voice: Can India's manufacturing sector avoid competition with China?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 23:18:00
India China Illustration: Chen Xia/Global Times Can India become a global manufacturing powerhouse while keeping its distance from the world's largest free trade agreement, simply to avoid competition from China? As debate over India's participation in the pact resurfaces, this question is becoming harder to avoid. Critics of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) in India worry that joining the pact could expose Indian industries to Chinese goods without adequate tariff protection. Yet an interview published by The Indian Express on Monday presented a different perspective. Alan Bollard, former governor of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, suggested that India should reconsider joining the pact, noting that membership could help the country tap into the supply chains that have made China so competitive. China is among the members of the RCEP, whose economies account for about 30 percent of global GDP, population and trade. Studies estimate that the agreement could add hundreds of billions of dollars to regional income and create millions of jobs by 2030. Whether India moves to join the RCEP is ultimately its own decision. But as the country seeks to strengthen its manufacturing base and expand its presence in overseas markets, broadening its network of free trade agreements can bring clear economic benefits. One such benefit is access to markets. The RCEP brings together dynamic economies in the Asia-Pacific, including China and South Korea, offering exporters easier access to a broad regional market. At a time when rising protectionism is making access to some developed economies more difficult, the pact offers considerable economic value to countries seeking to diversify their export destinations and tap into Asia's growing market opportunities. Another benefit that is easy to overlook is participation in regional supply chains. Consider a hypothetical example: wool imported from Australia and New Zealand could be processed into fabric in China, then sent to India, where it is made into garments for export to Japan and South Korea. The RCEP could help lower trade costs along this cross-border production chain, making it easier for businesses to organize production across several economies. India's imports of fabric from China would serve as inputs for higher-value garment exports, allowing the country to capture more value through manufacturing and create jobs. The question is not simply how much India imports from China, but how much it can gain by taking part in regional production networks. This offers a more productive path than remaining outside them. As technology advances, supply chains in the Asia-Pacific region are becoming more sophisticated, specialized and interconnected. The more efficient these networks become, the higher the cost of remaining outside them. Bollard's remarks offer a useful perspective: part of China's manufacturing competitiveness stems from its effective use of supply chains across Southeast Asia and South Korea. For other economies, participating in these networks can also strengthen their own manufacturing capabilities. Whether or not India seeks to join the RCEP, the direction of its efforts is likely to be much the same: finding more export opportunities in Asia-Pacific markets and becoming more deeply integrated into the region's production networks, including those linked to China. For a country seeking to expand its manufacturing base and reach more overseas markets, participation in these networks is part of the efforts to build a globally competitive manufacturing sector. Deeper integration also comes with greater competitive pressure. Greater integration will expose Indian manufacturers to more competition, not only from Chinese products but also from goods made in other RCEP economies. This may create short-term pressure for some industries. But slowing international integration to avoid competition would carry costs of its own. The answer to competitive pressure is not to retreat from regional production networks, but to build stronger capabilities through greater participation in them. Protecting industries from competition cannot substitute for making them more competitive. India's commitment to developing its manufacturing sector and expanding its global reach is clear. Whether or not it joins the RCEP, closer integration with regional supply chains, including those linked to China, will remain an important part of that journey. The RCEP could offer India a faster route to its destination. The question is whether India is ready to get on board.
